Calls to roxy's [host services](/reference/host-services), such as
writing state or adding a tag, run alongside the traffic rather than in
it. If addon A writes state that addon B should read, A must wait for its
write to finish before passing on the bytes B will read them with. A WASM
addon's calls always finish before it carries on. A service layer waits
for the `result` itself.

<img src={layerOrdering} alt="Two enforce layers, A and B, in roxy's request path, left to right, then the rules. The client's head (a solid line) and body bytes (a dashed line) run through A, then B, then to the rules; between A and B, a chunk reaches B once A sends it. Part-way through the body, A calls state_put, drawn as an arrow down to a host services strip along the bottom with a result arrow back up, and the note awaits result, then sends on; A's body line is broken at that point. In B, on the chunk that followed, a state_get arrow goes down to the strip and a result comes back, with the note on that chunk: sees A's write. A dotted line between the two calls says ordered only by A's wait. The strip lists host services: add_tag, state_put, state_get, record, and more." />

For the rules to see a tag or state write when they decide on the
request, it must land before the addon passes the request on. A later
write is seen by the next rule that reads it, but never changes a decision
already made.

## Modes

* `mode: enforce` (the default): the addon is in the path, and what it
  does takes effect.
* `mode: observe`: the addon gets a copy of the traffic and cannot change
  or delay it. Its failures are logged, never fatal. This is the way to
  try out a new monitor. An observer that falls too far behind loses its
  copy, and the exchange carries on
  ([observers](/reference/addon-configuration#observers)).

# Performance

On ordinary HTTP traffic roxy is on a par with Envoy. Doing TLS
interception it handles 3 to 20 times the requests per core of mitmproxy,
with a median latency in milliseconds rather than hundreds of
milliseconds.

| requests per core, roxy relative to | 1 KiB | 64 KiB | 1 MiB |
|---|---|---|---|
| Envoy, as a gateway | 1.3x | 1.0x | 0.8x |
| Envoy, as an egress proxy | 1.5x | 1.3x | 1.3x |
| mitmproxy, doing TLS interception | 19x | 8x | 2.7x |

## What an addon costs

roxy spends about 100 µs of CPU on a small exchange with no addons. An
addon that does nothing adds roughly another 100 µs, whether it is a WASM
component or a service. So an addon that does T µs of work makes an
exchange cost about 200 + T µs: four cores give roughly 20,000 requests a
second with no work, 13,000 at 100 µs and 4,000 at 800 µs. A service
layer's own CPU comes on top.

Bodies cost about 3 µs per KiB through a WASM layer and 4.5 µs per KiB
through a service layer, even when the layer leaves them untouched. A
1 MiB response through a do-nothing layer costs 4 to 5 ms, against about
0.6 ms with no addons.

| throughput lost to a do-nothing layer, as an egress proxy | 1 KiB | 64 KiB | 1 MiB |
|---|---|---|---|
| WASM layer | about 50% | about 70% | about 85% |
| service layer (sidecar on localhost) | about 60% | about 75% | about 90% |

## What is not measured

These figures come from one machine. No run uses body rules, capture,
body digests or a real addon. A body digest costs about one core per
400 MB/s on a CPU without SHA extensions, which is why it is opt-in.

# Configuration

One YAML file, starting `version: 1`. Each section is described on the
page the table names.

| key | page |
|---|---|
| `listeners`, `http` | [HTTP](/reference/http) |
| `ca_server`, `tls` | [managing the CA](/guides/ca-certificates), [TLS](/reference/tls) |
| `upstream` | [upstream](/reference/upstream), [address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor) |
| `address_lists` | [address lists](/reference/address-lists#address-lists) |
| `limits` | [resource limits](/reference/limits) |
| `rules` | [policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation), [rule language](/reference/rule-language) |
| `secrets` | [secrets](/reference/secrets) |
| `metrics` | [rate limits](/reference/rate-limits) |
| `addons` | [addon configuration](/reference/addon-configuration) |
| `log`, `capture_dir` | [flow log](/reference/flow-log) |
| `valid_until` | [lease](/guides/operations#lease) |

* Parsing is strict. An unknown key, or a key repeated in one map, is an
  error.
* Only `true` and `false` are booleans; `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are
  refused. Anchors and aliases work; merge keys (`<<`) and custom tags do
  not. A file holds one YAML document.
* Relative paths resolve against the working directory.
* `roxy check` refuses zero for a limit where zero would refuse every
  request. Body, message and capture caps and timeouts accept zero and
  mean it ([resource limits](/reference/limits#limits)).

```yaml
version: 1

listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy      # the default; `http` serves origin-form requests directly
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128

secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline stripped
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control-plane lease; standalone `run` refuses it

metrics:
  - id: github_writes
    count: requests
    where: host under "api.github.com" and method in [POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE]
    key: [client.ip]
    window: 1m

rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
      - allow

  - id: no-writes-burst
    when: metric.github_writes >= 30
    then: { deny: { status: 429 } }

  - id: upload-cap               # reads body.bytes: re-checked in flight
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and body.bytes > 10mb
    then: { deny: { status: 413 } }
```

# Rule language

The expressions used in a rule's `when` and a metric's `where`, and the
actions of a rule's `then`. How rules are evaluated is in
[policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation).

## Expressions

Expressions are statically typed, and regular expressions run in linear
time.

```
expr        := or
or          := and ( "or" and )*
and         := not ( "and" not )*
not         := "not" not | primary
primary     := "(" expr ")" | comparison | predicate
comparison  := operand OP operand
predicate   := field | bool                  ; boolean field, or a literal (`where: true`)
operand     := field | field "[" string "]" | literal
OP          := "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">="
             | "in" | "not in"
             | "starts_with" | "ends_with" | "contains"
             | "like"        ; glob, full match ( * ? )
             | "matches"     ; regex, full match
             | "under"       ; host == X or host ends_with "." + X
literal     := string | number [unit] | bool | list | ip | cidr | @list | method | "null"
list        := "[" literal ("," literal)* "]"
unit        := kb | mb | gb | ms | s | m | h      ; sizes are 1024-based
method      := [A-Z][A-Z_]*                       ; HTTP method names only
```

* A rule without `when` matches everything. So does a metric without
  `where`.
* Strings are double-quoted, with `\"` and `\\` escapes.
* Comparison is exact, except that `host`, `tls.sni` and `scheme` compare
  without regard to case, and so do header names. Header values are
  compared exactly. `method` is case-sensitive: `get` does not match
  `GET`.
* Mistakes are compile errors: a type mismatch (`host under 443`), a
  regex that does not compile, an unknown metric or `@list`, a
  `${secret:name}` placeholder in a condition, or a comparison that can
  never match, such as a `host` with a trailing dot or in upper case.

### Fields

*Admission* fields are known when roxy decides whether to forward the
request. *In-flight* fields become known later, and a rule that reads one
is checked as the exchange streams
([evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation#when-rules-run)).

| field | type | known |
|---|---|---|
| `client.ip` | ip | admission |
| `listener.name` | string | admission |
| `tls.sni`, `tls.alpn`, `tls.version` | string | admission |
| `method`, `scheme`, `host`, `port`, `path`, `url` | string / int | admission |
| `query["k"]`, `query.raw` | string | admission |
| `header["name"]`, `header.all["name"]` | string, list | admission |
| `body.size` | int: declared length, `null` if not declared | admission |
| `body.text` | string: the buffered body | admission |
| `metric.<id>` | int | admission ([rate limits](/reference/rate-limits#metrics)) |
| `state["key"]`, `tag["name"]` | string, bool | admission |
| `body.bytes` | int: request body bytes so far | in-flight |
| `response.status`, `response.header["name"]`, `response.header.all["name"]` | int, string, list | in-flight |
| `response.body.size` | int: declared length, `null` if not declared | in-flight |
| `response.body.text` | string: the buffered response body | in-flight |
| `response.body.bytes` | int: response body bytes so far | in-flight |
| `ws.direction`, `ws.opcode`, `ws.size`, `ws.text` | string, int, int, string | in-flight, per WebSocket message ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets#message-rules)) |

`client.ip` is the client's address, or behind a load balancer the one
`X-Forwarded-For` names
([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)). `host` and
`tls.sni` are lower-case, without a trailing dot, with internationalised
names as `xn--` labels and IPv6 addresses without brackets. `path` is
normalised ([URL normalisation](/reference/http#url-normalisation)).

**Path rules are fragile.** An upstream may interpret a path differently
from roxy, for example by decoding `%2F` to `/` or merging `//`. Then
`/a/..%2Fsecret` does not start with `/secret` for roxy, but reaches
`/secret` upstream. Prefer allowing exact paths. If you allow a prefix,
also exclude the forms the upstream reinterprets (`not path contains
"%2F"`, and likewise `"%5C"`, `"//"`, `";"` and `"%3B"`). Treat a `deny`
on a path as defence in depth.

### Missing values (`null`)

A value that is absent is `null`: a header or query parameter that was not
sent, an unset state key, `tls.sni` when none was sent, `body.size` for a
chunked body. Tags and metrics are never `null`.

| expression, with `x` missing | result |
|---|---|
| `x == null` | true |
| `x != null` | false |
| `x == "a"`, `x in [...]` | false |
| `x != "a"`, `x not in [...]` | true |
| any other operator, such as `x > 10` or `x contains "a"` | the exchange is denied: `_fail_closed`, reason `missing_value` |

`and` and `or` stop as soon as the result is known, so test for `null`
first: `body.size != null and body.size > 10mb`, or
`body.size == null or body.size > 1`.

## Actions

`then` is one action, or a list ending with at most one of `allow`, `deny`
or `quarantine`.

```yaml
then: allow
then: { deny: { status: 451, message: "no" } }
then:
  - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
  - remove_header: [x-debug]
  - tag: billing
  - allow: { upgrade: websocket }
```

These decide the exchange:

| action | where | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `allow` | admission rules | Forward the request. `upgrade: websocket` allows a WebSocket upgrade. `private_ok: true` allows private addresses ([address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)). |
| `deny` | all rules | Refuse, with `status` (default 403), `message` and `close` ([deny responses](/reference/http#deny-responses)). In flight, it stops the exchange. On a WebSocket, it closes both sides. |
| `quarantine` | all rules | Deny, and [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine) roxy so it refuses every later request. Needs `--state-dir`. |

These add effects:

| action | where | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `set_header: { name: value }` | request: admission rules; response: in-flight rules | Set or replace a header. Request values may use `${secret:name}` ([secrets](/reference/secrets)). |
| `remove_header: [names]` | as `set_header` | Remove headers. |
| `rewrite_path: { match, to }` | admission rules | Rewrite the path with a regex; `$1` and `${name}` refer to groups. |
| `set_query: { k: v }`, `remove_query: [k]` | admission rules | Change the query. |
| `redirect: { host, port, scheme?, rewrite_host? }` | admission rules | Send the request to another upstream. `Host` is unchanged unless `rewrite_host: true`. The new address still passes the address floor. |
| `tag: name` | all | Set `tag["name"]`, for later rules, addons and the log. |
| `log: { level, message }` | all | Write a `log` event to the flow log. |
| `set_state: { key, value, ttl? }` | all | Write to the [state store](/reference/rate-limits#state). |
| `capture: request \| response \| both` | admission rules | Record the exchange in the [capture log](/reference/flow-log#capture). |
| `digest: request \| response \| both` | admission rules | Record a SHA-256 of the bodies in the [flow log](/reference/flow-log#flow-log). |
| `sign: { aws_sigv4: { ... } }` | admission rules | Sign the request for AWS ([signing AWS requests](/reference/secrets#signing-aws-requests)). |

Anything more complex needs an addon.

## Body rules

`body.text` and `response.body.text` are the only fields that make roxy
buffer. If any rule reads `body.text`, roxy buffers every request body, up
to `limits.max_inspect_body_bytes` (1 MiB), before deciding, then streams
it on. `response.body.text` does the same for responses.

A body over the cap cannot be inspected, and a rule that reads it denies
the exchange (`body_too_large_to_inspect`). To let large bodies through,
raise the cap, or check the size before the text:

```yaml
when: body.size != null and body.size < 1mb and body.text contains "secret"
```

The text is the body decoded from its `content-encoding`
([content codings](/reference/http#content-codings)). A body that cannot
be decoded also denies the exchange.

# Secrets

`secrets:` maps names to where their values come from. `${secret:name}`
in a rule's `set_header` value, in `sign` credentials, or in an addon
endpoint's `headers` injects the value, so the client only ever holds a
placeholder. A reference anywhere else is a compile error.

```yaml
secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline is stripped
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control plane

rules:
  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # replaces whatever the client sent
      - allow
```

* Each secret has exactly one of `env`, `file` or `lease: true`.
* `env` and `file` are read at startup and on reload. A missing or empty
  value stops roxy starting, or fails a reload. `roxy check` and
  `roxy rule test` do not read them.
* Injected values are removed from the flow log and from captured headers.
* A `redirect` sends the request, injected values included, to the new
  target. Make sure a rule that injects a secret cannot match a request
  that another rule redirects elsewhere.

## Signing AWS requests

The `sign` action signs the forwarded request with AWS Signature Version
4, so a client holding placeholder credentials reaches AWS with a real
signature.

```yaml
secrets:
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }
  aws_token: { env: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN }

rules:
  - id: bedrock
    when: host under "bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com" and scheme == "https"
    then:
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
            session_token: "${secret:aws_token}"   # optional
      - allow
```

* roxy signs the request as it is forwarded, after every other change the
  rules make, wherever `sign` appears in `then`. It removes any signature
  headers the client sent first.
* `service` is the AWS signing name, such as `bedrock`, `s3` or
  `execute-api`. S3 services get S3's variant of the signature.
* A request with a presigned URL (`X-Amz-Signature` in the query) is
  forwarded under the client's signature, not roxy's. The rule's `host`
  and `path` conditions still limit where it can go.
* The body is buffered, up to `limits.max_sign_body_bytes` (100 MiB), to
  hash it. A larger body is refused with `413`. For S3,
  `unsigned_payload: true` skips the hash and streams the body.
* If two matching rules both sign, the request is denied
  (`sign_conflict`).

## Lease secrets

`name: { lease: true }` declares a secret that the control plane supplies
with the lease ([node protocol](/reference/node-protocol#lease-body)). It
is held in memory only, never on disk. `roxy run --config` refuses a
config that declares one. When the control plane changes a secret, the
next request uses the new value, while an exchange in progress keeps the
value it started with.

# Rate limits and state

Metrics count requests or bytes over a sliding window, for rules to
compare against. State is a key/value store that rules write with
`set_state` and read as `state["key"]`.

## Metrics

A metric is defined once and compared in rules, for example
`metric.github_writes >= 30`.

```yaml
metrics:
  - id: github_writes
    count: requests      # requests | request_bytes | response_bytes | errors | denied | unique(<field>)
    where: host under "api.github.com" and method in [POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE]
    key: [client.ip]     # one count per client; omitted = one count for everything
    window: 1m           # omitted = since start
    max_keys: 10000      # optional; default limits.max_metric_keys
```

* **`count`** says what is counted. `unique(<field>)` counts distinct
  values, approximately.
* **`where`** says which exchanges count. It can read admission fields,
  state and other metrics, but not tags.
* **`key`** gives each distinct value its own count. It takes plain
  admission fields such as `client.ip` or `host`, not headers.
* **Windows** slide in 60 steps, so a 1-minute window moves every second.
  A limit can trip up to one step early, never late.
* **Request counts** are read before the decision and updated after it, so
  `metric.x >= 30` denies the 31st request. Denied requests count too.
* **Byte counts** grow as bodies stream. A `deny` that reads one is
  checked as bytes arrive, and stops the exchange that crosses the limit.
* **Nullable fields.** If a key can be `null`, such as `tls.sni` on plain
  HTTP, the metric must exclude those exchanges in `where`
  (`tls.sni != null`), or it does not compile. A rule that reads the
  metric needs the same guard.
* **Reload.** A metric keeps its counts across a reload if its `id`,
  `count`, `where`, `key` and `window` are unchanged.

### Key cardinality

Each key value is a separate series, and the number of series is bounded
by `limits.max_metric_keys` (100 000), each metric's `max_keys`, and
`limits.max_metric_bytes`. Nothing is evicted to make room: once a table
is full, any request that needs a new series is denied
(`metric_table_full`) until old series expire
([never evict](/design/threat-model#never-evict)).

So be careful keying on values the client chooses. `host`, `path`, `url`
and `query.raw` are all chosen by the client, and denied requests count,
so a client can fill a table keyed on one of them without a single
request being allowed. Limit the values with `where`:

```yaml
metrics:
  - id: github_requests
    count: requests
    where: host in ["api.github.com", "github.com"]
    key: [host]
    window: 1m
```

`host under "github.com"` does not limit `host`, since the client also
chooses subdomains. Where the values cannot be listed, give the metric its
own `max_keys`, so that filling it only affects that metric. `roxy check`
warns about a metric keyed on a client-chosen field with no `where`.

## State

State is a key/value store shared by all exchanges. Each entry expires
after the rule's `ttl`, or one hour by default. A rule sees what earlier
exchanges wrote, and, within an exchange, what rules above it wrote. When
the store holds `limits.max_state_entries` (100 000) entries, a request
that needs a new key is denied (`state_unavailable`). Addons can read and
write the same store ([host services](/reference/host-services#state-state)).

# Address floor and lists

Rules decide by name. The address floor decides by IP address: before
roxy connects to an upstream, it checks every address the name resolved
to. Private addresses are refused by default, and address lists let you
refuse more. The settings are under `upstream` and `address_lists`
([upstream](/reference/upstream)).

## Address floor

roxy refuses to connect to an address if:

1. it is in `deny_cidrs`, which nothing can override; or
2. it is in one of the private ranges below, `deny_private_ranges` is on
   (the default), the address is not in `allow_cidrs`, and the rule that
   allowed the request does not say `private_ok: true`; or
3. it is in one of the lists named in `deny_lists`, which nothing can
   override.

| class | ranges |
|---|---|
| `unspecified` | `0.0.0.0/8`, `::` |
| `private` | `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16` (RFC 1918) |
| `shared` | `100.64/10` (CGNAT) |
| `loopback` | `127/8`, `::1` |
| `link_local` | `169.254/16`, `fe80::/10` |
| `documentation` | `192.0.2/24`, `198.51.100/24`, `203.0.113/24`, `2001:db8::/32` |
| `benchmarking` | `198.18/15` |
| `multicast` | `224/4`, `ff00::/8` |
| `reserved` | `192.0.0/24`, `240/4` |
| `unique_local` | `fc00::/7` |
| `site_local` | `fec0::/10` |
| `discard` | `100::/64` |

The check is on the address roxy actually connects to, so DNS rebinding
does not get around it. It applies to IP addresses in URLs, `redirect`
targets and addon endpoints too.

An IPv4 address can be written as an IPv6 address in several ways, for
example `::ffff:10.0.0.1`, or through NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`) or 6to4
(`2002::/16`). Denies match all of these forms. `allow_cidrs` only matches
the plain form of an address, so it cannot be used to sneak a private
address through.

A refused connection gets `403` with `terminal_rule: _address_policy`, and
an `upstream_denied` event in the flow log names the address and the
range or list that matched.

## Address lists

Address lists are named sets of IP ranges. They can be used to refuse
connections (`upstream.deny_lists`) and in rules, as `@name`.

```yaml
address_lists:
  - name: blocked
    file: /etc/roxy/lists/blocked.txt    # one address or CIDR per line; `#` comments
  - name: cloud-metadata
    inline: [169.254.169.254/32, "fd00:ec2::254/128", 100.100.100.200/32]
```

* In rules, use `@name` after `in` or `not in` with an IP field:
  `client.ip in @internal`. In a rule, a list only matches the plain form
  of an address, since a rule may allow on it.
* Lists are fast to search: a million entries take about 11 MiB.
* A file larger than `limits.max_address_list_bytes` (256 MiB), or with a
  malformed line, fails to load.
* List files are watched and reloaded with the config.
* `roxy check` reports how many entries each list has. In
  `roxy rule test`, a list that fails to load makes every rule that reads
  it deny.

# WebSockets

roxy only allows a WebSocket upgrade when the allowing rule says
`allow: { upgrade: websocket }`. Under a plain `allow`, roxy removes the
upgrade headers and forwards the request as ordinary HTTP, so the
client's WebSocket library reports a failed handshake. Upgrades to other
protocols are always removed.

## Relay

roxy forwards the upgrade over HTTP/1.1 and sends the client the `101`
only once the upstream has accepted, so a failed upgrade is always an
error response.

| failure | result |
|---|---|
| the client's upgrade request is not a valid WebSocket handshake | `400`, `terminal_rule: _websocket`, reason `ws_bad_handshake` |
| the upstream does not answer within `limits.response_header_timeout` | `504` |
| the upstream answers something other than `101` | passed to the client as it is |
| the upstream's `101` is invalid | `502` |

Through a proxy listener, use `wss://`. A `ws://` URL means plain HTTP
inside a CONNECT tunnel, which roxy refuses unless
`http.allow_plain_in_connect` is on. WebSockets over HTTP/2 are not
supported, so clients use HTTP/1.1 for them.

If no rule reads a `ws.*` field, roxy passes the bytes through as they
are. Either way:

* WebSocket bytes count towards byte metrics, so a byte limit can close a
  WebSocket.
* Capture records both directions.
* Addons sit between the client and the relay, so rules and capture see
  what the addons pass on.
* A WebSocket with no traffic for `limits.idle_timeout` (1 h) is closed.
* The flow log records `ws_open` and `ws_close`, with byte counts.

## Extensions

A compressed WebSocket message cannot be read on its own, so when
anything needs to read messages, roxy removes the client's offer of
compression. That is when a rule reads `ws.*`, or when an addon runs on
the upgrade and decodes bodies (the default;
[addons](/reference/addon-configuration#content-codings)). Otherwise
extensions pass through.

## Message rules

Rules that read `ws.*` are checked on every message after the upgrade:

```yaml
rules:
  - id: chat
    when: host == "chat.example.com"
    then: { allow: { upgrade: websocket } }
  - id: no-keys-out
    when: ws.direction == "c2s" and ws.opcode == 1 and ws.text matches ".*sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}.*"
    then: deny
```

| field | value |
|---|---|
| `ws.direction` | `c2s` (client to upstream) or `s2c` |
| `ws.opcode` | 1 text, 2 binary, 8 close, 9 ping, 10 pong |
| `ws.size` | payload length in bytes |
| `ws.text` | a text message's text; `null` for other messages |

`ws.text` is `null` for pings and other control messages, so start text
rules with `ws.opcode == 1 and ...`
([missing values](/reference/rule-language#missing-values-null)).
Otherwise the first ping closes the WebSocket.

A matching deny closes both sides with code `1008`. Rules cannot drop or
change a single message; that needs an addon.

### Parsing

With message rules, roxy checks each message strictly against the
WebSocket spec, reassembles fragmented messages up to
`limits.max_ws_message_bytes` (16 MiB), and checks that text is valid
UTF-8. It forwards each message once it is complete, as a single frame.
A protocol error closes both sides with `1002`, `1007` for invalid UTF-8,
or `1009` for a message over the limit.

### Logging

A denied message is logged as a `ws_message` event. With
`log.flow.ws_message_every: N`, every Nth message is logged as well.
Message contents are never logged.

# HTTP

How clients talk to roxy, how requests are parsed, and what goes to the
upstream and back.

## Listener modes

| mode | the client speaks | request target |
|---|---|---|
| `http_proxy` (default) | HTTP/1.1 to a proxy (`HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY`) | absolute-form, or CONNECT and then origin-form inside the tunnel |
| `http` | plain HTTP/1.1 to roxy as if it were the server | origin-form; `Host` names the target |

roxy does not authenticate clients. Rules see `listener.name` and
`client.ip`.

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy           # the default
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
    quarantine_on:             # optional
      parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for:             # optional; mode: http only
      trusted_hops: 1          # the proxies in front of roxy
```

`quarantine_on.parse_errors` [quarantines](/guides/operations#quarantine)
roxy once the listener has refused `count` malformed requests within
`window`. It needs `roxy run --state-dir`.

## HTTP proxy

* **Absolute-form** (`GET http://host/path HTTP/1.1`) is plain HTTP.
  `Host` must match the URL.
* **CONNECT** opens a tunnel that roxy inspects ([below](/reference/http#connect)).
* **Origin-form** is refused, except for the host `roxy.internal`, which
  serves the CA at `/roxy-ca.pem`
  ([CA distribution](/guides/ca-certificates#ca-distribution)).
* `Proxy-Authorization` is never forwarded.

## HTTP listener

For a gateway behind a load balancer that terminates TLS
([HTTP gateway](/guides/gateway)).

* Only origin-form requests are accepted.
* `Host` names the target: exactly one, port 80 unless given, scheme
  `http`. Without a `redirect` the request goes to that host over plain
  HTTP.
* A client that starts a TLS handshake is closed
  (`tls_on_http_listener`).

### Clients behind a load balancer

Without `forwarded_for`, `client.ip` is the TCP peer, which behind a load
balancer is the load balancer. With `forwarded_for.trusted_hops: N`, each
of the N proxies in front of roxy is taken to append the address it saw
to `X-Forwarded-For`, so the client is the Nth entry from the right.
Entries further left were written by the client and are ignored.

* That address is `client.ip` everywhere: rules, metric keys, addons and
  the flow log. The flow log also records the TCP peer as `client.peer`.
* A request with fewer entries than hops, or with a trusted entry that is
  not a plain IP address, is refused with `400`
  (`forwarded_for_invalid`). It is never attributed to the peer instead.
* The header is forwarded as received.

The hop count does not prove that a request came through those proxies.
A client that can reach the listener directly can write its own entries,
so the network must let only the trusted proxies reach the listener.

## CONNECT

A CONNECT gets `200 Connection Established`. Rules decide on the requests
inside the tunnel. The tunnel's first bytes must be:

* **A TLS ClientHello.** With `tls.require_sni_match` (default true) the
  SNI must name the CONNECT host (`sni_mismatch`). roxy terminates TLS
  with a certificate for that host, then reads HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.
* **Plain HTTP**, only with `http.allow_plain_in_connect` (default
  false).

Anything else is closed, so raw TCP never passes. Requests inside the
tunnel must name the CONNECT host.

## HTTP/2

roxy offers HTTP/2 inside TLS tunnels (`http.enable_h2`, default true).
Upstream, it uses HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1, whichever the origin chooses.
WebSocket upgrades always use HTTP/1.1
([WebSockets](/reference/websockets)).

### Informational responses

roxy does not relay `1xx` responses from upstream, such as
`103 Early Hints`. It sends its own `100 Continue` once the rules allow an
upload.

### Trailers

`http.allow_response_trailers` (default true) forwards an origin's
response trailers, so gRPC works. `http.allow_request_trailers` (default
false) accepts trailers on requests; without it, a request with trailers
is refused (`trailers`). Request trailers arrive after the rules have
decided, which is why they are opt-in, and can only be forwarded to an
HTTP/2 origin.

A trailer may not carry framing, routing, authentication or `content-*`
fields. A request with one is refused. A response with one is ended
early, so the client never sees it as complete.

## Rejection rules

A malformed request closes the connection and logs a `parse_error` event
with a stable reason code. The settings under `http:` default to strict.
The same checks apply to HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and requests an addon passes on.

### Request line

* The method is a token of at most 32 bytes.
* The version is `HTTP/1.1`. `HTTP/1.0` needs `http.allow_http10`.
* Lines end in CRLF. A bare LF or CR anywhere in the head is refused.
* The head is at most `limits.max_header_bytes` (64 KiB) and the URL at
  most `limits.max_url_bytes` (8 KiB).

### Headers

* No whitespace before the colon, no folded lines.
* Values are visible ASCII, space and tab. Control characters are
  refused. Bytes above 127 need `http.allow_obs_text`, and rules read
  each as one ISO-8859-1 character.
* At most `limits.max_headers` (100) fields.
* Exactly one `Host`, matching the URL or the CONNECT host.
* A host is a DNS name in ASCII (internationalised names as `xn--`
  labels), an IPv4 address, or a bracketed IPv6 address.
* At most one `Content-Length`, digits only. A duplicate is refused even
  with the same value.
* `Transfer-Encoding`, if present, is exactly `chunked`, and never
  together with `Content-Length`.
* GET, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE may carry a body only with
  `http.allow_body_on_get` (`body_on_bodiless_method`).
* `Expect` may only be `100-continue`; anything else gets `417`.
* Hop-by-hop fields (`Connection` and the fields it names, `Keep-Alive`,
  `Proxy-Connection`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Proxy-Authenticate`, `TE`,
  `Trailer`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Upgrade`) are never forwarded.
  `Upgrade` is honoured only for a WebSocket a rule allows.

### Body

* Chunk extensions need `http.allow_chunk_extensions`.
* A body is at most `limits.max_request_body_bytes` (1 GiB).
* Timeouts are in [limits](/reference/limits#limits).

### HTTP/2 requests

* The pseudo-headers appear exactly once each, before other headers.
* Connection-specific headers reset the stream. `te` is accepted only as
  `trailers`.
* `:path` is normalised like an HTTP/1.1 target. `:authority` must match
  the CONNECT host, and so must `host` if present.
* `limits.h2_max_concurrent_streams` and `limits.h2_max_header_list_bytes`
  cap streams per connection and header bytes per stream.

## URL normalisation

Applied to the request target, for matching and forwarding alike.

1. The path starts with `/`. Percent-encodings must be well formed.
   `[ ] { } | ^` are percent-encoded. Space, control characters, `"`, `<`,
   `>`, `\`, a backtick and non-ASCII are refused.
2. Percent-encoded unreserved characters (`A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~`) are
   decoded. Other encodings stay as they are: `%2F` stays `%2F`.
3. Hex digits in the remaining encodings are upper-cased.
4. Dot segments are removed, including encoded ones. A path that climbs
   above the root is refused.
5. An empty path becomes `/`.
6. The query is validated the same way, but nothing in it is decoded.
7. A fragment is refused.
8. The host is lower-cased, its trailing dot removed, and the port made
   explicit.

## Upstream requests

roxy writes the request out in one canonical form, over HTTP/2 or
HTTP/1.1. Changes made by rules and addons pass the same validation as
the client's request: a header value containing a line break denies the
exchange.

## Responses

Upstreams are trusted ([threat model](/design/threat-model)), but roxy
re-frames every response: hop-by-hop fields are removed and the framing
rebuilt. Redirects are forwarded, not followed. Compressed bodies pass
through unchanged. Size and time limits are in
[limits](/reference/limits#limits).

## Content codings

roxy decodes `content-encoding` only to inspect a body. `body.text` and
`response.body.text` see the decoded text, while the bytes forwarded are
the bytes received ([body rules](/reference/rule-language#body-rules)).
Addons are the exception: by default they get decoded bodies
([content codings for addons](/reference/addon-configuration#content-codings)).

roxy decodes `gzip`, `x-gzip`, `deflate`, `br` and `zstd`, stacked up to
four deep. Decoding is strict: a truncated or corrupt body cannot be
inspected, and a rule that reads it fails closed.

`http.strip_accept_encoding` (default false) removes `accept-encoding`
from every request, so origins answer uncompressed.

## Deny responses

Every refusal roxy makes has the same shape:

```
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
content-type: application/json
cache-control: no-store
x-roxy-rule: <rule id>
connection: close

{"error":"blocked by roxy","rule":"<rule id>","flow":"<flow id>"}
```

| refusal | status | `rule` |
|---|---|---|
| a rule denies | `403`, or the rule's `deny.status` | the rule id |
| roxy is quarantined | `403` | `_quarantined` |
| address floor | `403` | `_address_policy` |
| unavailable policy input | `503` | `_fail_closed` |
| failed addon | `503` | `layer:<name>` |
| upstream failure | `502` (`504` for a timeout) | none |

The response never says why. The reason is in the flow log only.

A malformed request is refused before any rule sees it, with its reason:

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
content-type: application/json
connection: close

{"error":"rejected by roxy","reason":"cl_and_te"}
```

The status is `400`, or a closer one for the reason (`413`, `414`,
`431`). On HTTP/2 the stream is reset instead.

A rule sets the status and message with
`deny: { status: 451, message: "..." }`. After a deny the connection is
closed, unless the rule says `deny: { close: false }`. After an upstream
failure the connection stays open.

# Upstream

How roxy reaches the origin: it resolves names itself, checks every
address against the [address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor),
and verifies the origin's TLS certificate.

```yaml
upstream:
  dns:
    resolver: system           # system | [ "1.1.1.1:53", ... ]
    cache_ttl_cap: 60s         # the longest roxy caches an answer
    static_hosts: {}           # name: ip, used before DNS; still checked by the address floor
  deny_private_ranges: true
  deny_cidrs: []               # never connect to these
  allow_cidrs: []              # exceptions to the private ranges only
  deny_lists: [blocked]        # names from address_lists
  connect_timeout: 10s         # for the TCP connection, then again for the TLS handshake
  max_h2_connections_per_origin: 4

tls:
  upstream:
    verify: strict             # strict | strict+extra_roots
    extra_roots: []            # PEM files
    min_version: "1.2"         # "1.2" | "1.3"
```

`deny_cidrs` and `allow_cidrs` entries must be networks: `roxy check`
refuses `10.1.2.3/8` and suggests `10.0.0.0/8`.

## DNS

roxy resolves upstream names itself, so the workload's DNS plays no part.
If a name has several addresses, roxy tries them in turn, alternating
IPv4 and IPv6, within one `connect_timeout`. The resolver is set up at
startup, so changing `upstream.dns` needs a
[restart](/guides/operations#restart-only-settings).

## Upstream TLS

roxy verifies every upstream certificate against the Mozilla root
certificates, plus `extra_roots` with `verify: strict+extra_roots`.
Verification cannot be turned off. The TLS handshake has its own
`connect_timeout`.

## Connections

roxy keeps connections to each origin open for reuse, and closes them
after 90 seconds idle. Over HTTP/1.1 it opens one connection per request
in progress. Over HTTP/2 it uses up to `max_h2_connections_per_origin`
connections and spreads requests across them.

If an HTTP/2 origin closes a connection before handling some requests,
roxy retries those without a body on another connection. A request with
a body gets `502`, since its body has already been sent.

## Errors

| failure | response | flow log |
|---|---|---|
| the address floor refuses the address | `403`, `_address_policy` | `upstream_denied` |
| DNS, connection or TLS failure | `502` | `upstream_error`, reason `dns_failed`, `connect_failed` or `tls_failed` |
| a target roxy cannot connect to | `502` | `upstream_error`, reason `invalid_target` |
| a timeout connecting, during the TLS handshake or waiting for the response | `504` | `upstream_error`, reason `timeout` |
| a response roxy cannot parse | `502` | `upstream_error`, reason `protocol_error` |

The client gets the usual refusal body
([deny responses](/reference/http#deny-responses)). The reason is in the
flow log only.

# TLS

How roxy speaks TLS to clients on a proxy listener. Setting up the CA is
in [managing the CA](/guides/ca-certificates).

## Leaf certificates

roxy creates a certificate for each host the first time a client
connects to it, signed by its CA. Certificates are ECDSA P-256 and valid
for seven days, or until the CA expires if that is sooner. roxy keeps up
to `tls.leaf_cache_size` of them.

## Client-facing TLS

* roxy picks the certificate by SNI, or by the CONNECT host if the client
  sends no SNI. An invalid SNI fails the handshake.
* Host names are compared in lower case without a trailing dot, so
  `CONNECT Example.COM.:443` with SNI `example.com` is one host.
* roxy offers HTTP/2 (with `http.enable_h2`) and HTTP/1.1.
* TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are supported. Sessions are not resumed.
* The handshake must finish within `limits.header_timeout`.

## ClientHello sniffing

After a CONNECT, roxy reads the first TLS message to confirm that the
tunnel carries TLS and to find the SNI. A ClientHello that is malformed,
over 16 KiB, or split across several TLS records is treated as not TLS,
and the connection is closed.

# Resource limits

When something goes wrong, roxy refuses the request or closes the
connection rather than letting traffic through
([fail closed](/design/threat-model#fail-closed)).

## Fail-closed outcomes

| condition | result |
|---|---|
| roxy is quarantined | `403`, `_quarantined` ([quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine)) |
| a malformed request | the connection is closed, with a `400` if possible, and a `parse_error` event |
| a rule denies | the deny response, then the connection is closed |
| a metric, address list or secret is unavailable | `503`, `_fail_closed` |
| a metric table is full | `503`, `_fail_closed`, `metric_table_full` |
| a body is too large to inspect, or cannot be decoded | `503`, `_fail_closed` |
| a body to sign is over `max_sign_body_bytes` | `413`, `_sign` |
| the buffer budget is used up | `503`, `_fail_closed`, `buffer_budget_exhausted` |
| a body or header limit is exceeded mid-stream | both sides are closed |
| the upstream cannot be resolved or reached, or fails TLS | `502` ([upstream](/reference/upstream#errors)) |
| the upstream times out | `504` |
| the address floor refuses the upstream | `403`, `_address_policy` |
| an enforcing addon fails | `503`, `layer:<name>` |
| a config reload fails | the old policy stays |
| a connection cap is reached | the new connection is refused |
| the flow log or capture falls behind | traffic waits until it catches up |

Reason codes are in the flow log only, never in the response.

## Limits

All are under `limits:`. Defaults are shown. Sizes are 1024-based.

```yaml
limits:
  # client requests
  max_header_bytes: 64kb
  max_url_bytes: 8kb
  max_headers: 100
  max_request_body_bytes: 1gb
  header_timeout: 10s             # to send each request head (and CONNECT, and the TLS handshake)
  body_idle_timeout: 10m          # the client stalls sending its body, or reading the response
  idle_timeout: 1h                # an idle keep-alive connection or WebSocket
  h2_max_concurrent_streams: 100
  h2_max_header_list_bytes: 64kb

  # responses
  max_response_body_bytes: 1gb
  response_header_timeout: 15m    # the upstream's response head, once the request body is sent
  response_body_idle_timeout: 30m # the upstream stalls mid-body

  # buffering
  max_inspect_body_bytes: 1mb     # body.text, response.body.text, and addons' default
  max_sign_body_bytes: 100mb      # a body hashed for sign: aws_sigv4
  max_capture_body_bytes: 16mb    # per direction per exchange
  max_ws_message_bytes: 16mb      # a WebSocket message, when rules read messages
  max_observer_lag_bytes: 16mb    # how far an observing addon may fall behind
  max_buffered_bytes: 1gb         # all of the above together, across the process

  # connections
  max_connections: 10000
  max_connections_per_client: 10000   # per client IP; defaults to max_connections

  # policy state
  max_metric_keys: 100000
  max_metric_bytes: 256mb
  max_state_entries: 100000
  max_address_list_bytes: 256mb
```

The upstream connection timeout is `upstream.connect_timeout`
([upstream](/reference/upstream)). Addons have their own limits
([addon limits](/reference/addon-configuration#limits)).

### Timeouts

The timeouts are generous by default. roxy decides what passes, not how
long a well-behaved exchange may take: a model call that takes minutes to
start answering, or a quiet WebSocket, should not hit one. Only
`header_timeout` is tight, to stop clients that open connections and send
nothing. A long timeout costs a connection slot, not memory, so if idle
connections run out, raise `max_connections` rather than shortening the
timeouts.

If the upstream answers before it has read the whole upload, and then
stops reading it for twice `body_idle_timeout`, roxy cancels the upload
and records `upstream_body_timeout`.

### Buffer budget

`max_buffered_bytes` bounds everything roxy buffers to inspect or copy:
bodies that rules read, bodies being decoded or signed, WebSocket messages
that rules read, endpoint call bodies, and copies for observing addons.
Each exchange reserves what it needs before it buffers. If the budget
cannot cover a reservation, the exchange fails at once
(`buffer_budget_exhausted`). Nothing waits and nothing is evicted.

A body of unknown length that a rule reads reserves the whole
`max_inspect_body_bytes`, so the defaults allow 1024 such bodies at once.
The budget is not a cap on the process's memory: socket buffers, streaming
buffers and addon memory are separate.

## Connections

* A connection over `max_connections` or `max_connections_per_client` is
  closed at once and logged as `connection_refused`. The per-client cap
  counts TCP peers, so behind a load balancer it counts the load
  balancer.
* The `ca_server` listener has a separate cap of `max_connections`.
* Each HTTP/2 connection can hold up to 4 MiB of request data not yet
  sent upstream, outside the buffer budget.
* Metric and state tables never evict entries
  ([never evict](/design/threat-model#never-evict)).

# Addon configuration

Addons are listed under `addons:`, in the order the request passes through them
([addon model](/design/addon-model)). Each entry is a WASM layer or a
service layer; the two kinds share most keys.

```yaml
addons:
  - name: sentinel
    kind: wasm
    path: /etc/roxy/addons/sentinel.wasm
    mode: enforce
    when: host == "api.anthropic.com" and path starts_with "/v1/messages"
    subscribe: { request: full, response: head }
    capabilities: [state, record, endpoints]
    endpoints:
      monitor-model:
        url: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
        headers: { x-api-key: "${secret:monitor_key}" }
        timeout: 10s
      threat-intel:
        url: https://ti.internal:8443/score
        path: prefix
        private_ok: true
    limits: { max_memory: 128mb, first_byte_timeout: 30s }
    config: { reject_at: 0.8 }

  - name: monitor
    kind: service
    endpoint: sidecar
    mode: observe
    sample: 0.1
    subscribe: { request: head, response: head }
    endpoints:
      sidecar: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000/layer", private_ok: true }
    limits: { first_byte_timeout: 2s, max_connections: 4, max_streams: 100 }
```

## Fields

"kind" says which kind of addon takes the key. `roxy check` refuses a key
on the other kind.

| key | kind | values | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | both | string, unique | required | names the addon in the flow log and in `layer:<name>` |
| `kind` | both | `wasm`, `service` | `wasm` | a WebAssembly component inside roxy, or an external service ([service layer protocol](/reference/service-layers)) |
| `path` | wasm | file path | required | the component. It is compiled when the config loads, and reused across reloads while it is unchanged |
| `endpoint` | service | one of this addon's `endpoints` | required | where the service is |
| `mode` | both | `enforce`, `observe` | `enforce` | whether the addon is in the path or gets a copy ([modes](/design/addon-model#modes)) |
| `when` | both | a rule condition | every exchange | runs the addon only on the exchanges it matches ([choosing exchanges](/reference/addon-configuration#choosing-exchanges)) |
| `sample` | both, observe only | number in (0, 1] | 1 | the share of matching exchanges an observer gets a copy of |
| `subscribe.request` | both | `head`, `full` | `full` | whether the addon sees the request body ([what a layer sees](/reference/addon-configuration#what-a-layer-sees)) |
| `subscribe.response` | both | `head`, `full` | `full` | the same for the response |
| `capabilities` | both | list | none | the [host services](/reference/host-services) the addon may use ([capabilities](/reference/addon-configuration#capabilities)) |
| `config` | both | any YAML value | `null` | passed to the addon as JSON; roxy does not read it |
| `endpoints` | both | map of name to [endpoint](/reference/addon-configuration#endpoints) | none | the URLs the addon may call |
| `limits` | both | [limits](/reference/addon-configuration#limits) | see below | what the addon may cost roxy |

### `endpoints`

Each endpoint is a URL roxy calls on the addon's behalf, with credentials
the addon never sees. Calls go straight to the upstream, not through
other addons or the rules, but the address floor still applies.

| key | values | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | `http(s)://host[:port][/path]` | required | the target |
| `path` | `fixed`, `prefix` | `fixed` | whether the addon's path is ignored or appended to the URL ([endpoints](/reference/host-services#endpoints-endpoints)) |
| `headers` | map of header to value | none | added by roxy, replacing any the addon set. Values may use `${secret:name}` ([secrets](/reference/secrets)) |
| `timeout` | duration | `30s` | from the call to the response head |
| `private_ok` | bool | `false` | allows a private, loopback or link-local address |

### `limits`

Limits are there to catch a broken addon, not a slow one. A slow addon
makes its exchanges slow, not refused.

| key | kind | default | what it bounds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `first_byte_timeout` | both | `30s` | how long the addon may hold a request or response head before passing it on or answering. Time spent waiting for the upstream does not count. It also bounds the wait for a free instance or connection. Going over fails the addon |
| `max_memory` | wasm | `64mb` | memory per instance. A Python interpreter in WASM needs 128 to 256 MiB |
| `max_instances` | wasm | `1024` | instances running at once, and so exchanges at once |
| `recycle_after_exchanges` | wasm | `10000` | an instance is replaced after this many exchanges; `0` replaces it after every one |
| `recycle_above_memory` | wasm | three quarters of `max_memory` | an instance using more memory than this is replaced after its exchange |
| `max_connections` | service | `4` | WebSocket connections to the service |
| `max_streams` | service | `100` | exchanges at once on one connection |

Once the addon has answered, its bodies are bound by the usual body idle
timeouts, not by `first_byte_timeout`. There is no total CPU budget.

### Fixed caps

These limits cannot be configured:

| cap | value | on overrun |
|---|---|---|
| a request or response head an addon passes on | 128 KiB, and at most [`limits.max_headers`](/reference/limits#limits) fields | fails the exchange |
| tags on an exchange, including the rules' | 64 tags, 4 KiB in all | fails the exchange |
| a log message, or a record | 64 KiB | fails the exchange |
| a body handed over in one piece | 1 MiB; larger bodies must be streamed | fails the exchange |
| an endpoint call's request body | 16 MiB | refuses the call |
| endpoint calls in progress per exchange | 8 | further calls wait |
| a state key, a state value | 1 KiB, 64 KiB | refuses the call |

`roxy check` refuses a `when` that reads `body.*`, `response.*` or
`ws.*`, a zero limit, `sample` on an enforcing addon, and
`recycle_above_memory` above `max_memory`.

## Capabilities

An addon can only reach roxy's host services that its `capabilities`
grant:

| capability | grants |
|---|---|
| `endpoints` | calls to the addon's `endpoints`. A service layer does not need it: it makes its own calls |
| `state` | reading and writing the [state store](/reference/rate-limits#state) |
| `record` | writing events to the flow log |
| `metrics` | reading metrics |
| `log` | writing to roxy's own log |
| `quarantine` | [quarantining](/guides/operations#quarantine) roxy; enforcing addons only |

Calling a service without its capability fails the addon. Reading the
exchange's details, adding tags and reading `config` need no capability,
but observers cannot add tags or write state. There is no capability for
secrets: credentials go in an endpoint's `headers`.

## Behaviour

### What a layer sees

`subscribe` sets what an addon gets of each direction. With `full`, the
default, the addon reads the body as it streams, and what it passes on is
the body that goes on. With `head`, the addon only gets the head, and the
body goes past it untouched.

* A head-only addon can still refuse, change or answer at the head. If it
  answers a response head with the status it was given, the upstream's
  body follows. If it answers with another status, its own (empty) body
  replaces the upstream's.
* A head-only addon cannot send a body of its own; trying to fails the
  exchange (`unsubscribed:request` or `unsubscribed:response`).
* A head-only observer costs no buffering.
* The rules judge the request that leaves the stack, head and body,
  whoever supplied each.

### Observers

An observer gets copies of the traffic and runs beside the exchange,
which does not wait for it. An observer that keeps up sees every body in
full. It loses its copy, and the exchange carries on, if it falls
`limits.max_observer_lag_bytes` behind, if the
[buffer budget](/reference/limits#buffer-budget) runs out, or if no
instance is free within its `first_byte_timeout`. Each of these logs an
`observer_lagged` event.

### Streaming protocols

Bodies stream through addons chunk by chunk, so streaming protocols work:

| protocol | notes |
|---|---|
| SSE, NDJSON, streaming JSON, multipart, HTTP-based MCP | Chunk boundaries need not match the protocol's messages, so an addon that edits messages has to parse them itself. |
| gRPC | Works, including trailers such as `grpc-status`. A WASM addon that copies a body into a new stream drops its trailers; passing the body through keeps them. |
| WebSockets | Supported over HTTP/1.1 ([below](/reference/addon-configuration#websockets)). |
| `1xx` responses | Not relayed. An addon sends one final response head. |
| other upgrades, raw TCP, WebTransport, HTTP/3 | Not supported. |

An addon that holds a streaming response for approval can send its own
`200 text/event-stream` head straight away, keep the connection alive
with SSE comments such as `: approval pending`, and then stream the
approved events. Once the head has gone, a refusal has to be an event in
the stream, not a new status.

### Choosing exchanges

`when` is a [rule language](/reference/rule-language) condition. An
addon runs only on the exchanges it matches, and the rest pass it at no
cost.

* `when` sees the request as it reaches the addon, after earlier addons
  have changed it.
* It can read request fields, state, metrics and address lists, but not
  bodies, responses or WebSocket messages.
* `tag["x"]` sees tags set by earlier addons, not by the rules, which run
  later.
* If an input it needs is unavailable, the exchange fails with `503`
  rather than skipping the addon.

`sample` is decided from the exchange's id, so the same exchange always
gets the same answer.

### In the flow log

| field | with addons |
|---|---|
| `addons` | the addons that ran, in order |
| `rules`, `decision`, `terminal_rule` | the rules' decision on the request that left the stack. `req` is what the client sent, and `res.status` what it got, which an addon may have changed |
| `decision: answered`, `terminal_rule: layer:<name>` | an addon answered the request itself |
| `terminal_rule: layer:<name>`, `reason: layer_error` | an addon failed; a `layer_error` event follows ([failure](/reference/addon-configuration#failure)) |

### Content codings

When an addon that reads bodies runs on an exchange, roxy decompresses
the bodies for it and removes `content-encoding`. The client then gets an
uncompressed response and the upstream an uncompressed request. Nothing
is compressed again. A body in a coding roxy does not know, or a partial
response (`206`), passes through as it is.

`http.decode_for_addons: false` turns this off, so addons see bodies as
sent.

### WebSockets

An addon gets a WebSocket's upgrade request like any other request, and
the upstream's `101` as the response. After that, the request body
carries the client's WebSocket frames and the response body the
upstream's, for as long as the WebSocket is open. The addon can read,
change or hold either direction, or refuse the upgrade by answering it.

* The addon must handle both directions at once, since the request body
  only ends when the client closes. The `roxy-addon` SDK does this.
* Frames from the client are masked, as the WebSocket protocol requires.
* An addon that turns the `101` into another status fails the exchange.

### Failure

Every failure is closed. If an enforcing addon crashes, goes over a
limit, uses a capability it lacks, passes on an invalid head, or never
answers, the exchange fails: with `503` and `terminal_rule:
layer:<name>` if the response has not started, and otherwise by closing
the connection before the response is complete. A `layer_error` event
records what went wrong in `kind`, such as `trap`, `budget:<limit>`,
`capability:<name>`, `invalid_request`, `invalid_response`,
`no_response` or `service:<code>`.

A client that disconnects cancels the exchange; that is not the addon's
failure. A WASM instance that failed is thrown away, never reused.

An addon that deliberately stops a body part way through, for example by
dropping a stream without finishing it, is not a failure. Nor is one that
stops reading the response from upstream, which cancels the request
upstream. The flow log records `layer_aborted`, and whoever reads that
body sees it end early.

#### Who is blamed

Only one party is blamed for a failed exchange: the first to fail.

* **An addon's own failure** is that addon's. A request an addon passed
  on that is invalid is blamed on that addon.
* **A client upload that breaks** is the client's, as without addons,
  even if an addon passed the broken body on.
* **An upstream response body that fails** is the upstream's
  (`upstream_body_failed`).
* **A body the buffer budget cannot cover** is the budget's
  (`buffer_budget_exhausted`).
* **An observer is never blamed.**

# Service layer protocol

A `kind: service` addon is an external service that each exchange streams
through, at its place in the [stack](/design/addon-model). roxy streams
the request to the service, and the service streams back the request to
forward, if it forwards one. roxy then streams the response from upstream
to the service, and the service streams back the response the client
gets. The service can pass bytes through, change them, hold them, or send
its own, in either direction, at any time.

```yaml
addons:
  - name: sentinel
    kind: service
    endpoint: sidecar                   # one of this addon's endpoints
    mode: enforce                       # enforce | observe
    endpoints:
      sidecar: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000/layer", private_ok: true }
    limits:
      first_byte_timeout: 2s
      max_connections: 4                # per endpoint
      max_streams: 100                  # exchanges at once per connection
```

The other keys are as for any addon
([addon configuration](/reference/addon-configuration)). For a minimal
service and a Python implementation of this protocol, see
[writing addons](/guides/writing-addons#a-service-layer).

## Transport

roxy keeps long-lived WebSocket connections to the service, each carrying
many exchanges at once. Each exchange is a **stream** on a connection.

* The WebSocket subprotocol is `roxy.layer.v7`. A service that does not
  accept it fails the handshake.
* roxy connects to the endpoint's URL (`http` becomes `ws`, `https`
  becomes `wss`), checked by the address floor, with the endpoint's
  `headers`.
* A new exchange uses an idle connection if there is one, otherwise opens
  a new one up to `max_connections`, otherwise shares the least busy
  connection. Each connection is read and written in order, so a service
  that handles each connection on one task gets one core per connection.
* If a connection fails, the exchanges on it fail. Later exchanges use
  another connection.
* After a reload, new exchanges use new connections, and old connections
  close once their exchanges finish.

### Frames

Text frames are JSON messages, each with a `stream` field. Binary frames
are body bytes: a 4-byte big-endian stream id, one byte for the direction
(`0` request body, `1` response body), then the bytes. roxy numbers the
streams on a connection from 1 upwards and never reuses a number.

A stream starts with an `open` message from roxy:

```json
{"type":"open","stream":7,"flow":"01J…","conn":"01J…","layer":"sentinel",
 "mode":"enforce","subscribe":{"request":"full","response":"head"},
 "client_ip":"10.0.0.5","listener":"proxy",
 "sni":"api.example.com","tags":["a","b"],
 "capabilities":["state","record"],"config":{"reject_at":0.8}}
```

`client_ip` is `client.ip` as rules see it. `sni` is left out when there
is none. `capabilities` and `config` are the addon's. `flow` and `layer`
together identify the exchange and addon, so a service can key its state
on them.

The rest of the exchange, with `stream` left out:

```text
roxy → service   {"type":"request","method":…,"url":…,"headers":[[n,v],…]}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}
service → roxy   {"type":"request",…}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}       the request to forward, at most once
                 {"type":"request_end"} alone                             forward nothing
roxy → service   {"type":"response","status":…,"headers":[…]}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}
                                                                          the response to what the service forwarded
                 {"type":"response_end"} alone                            no response: nothing was forwarded, or the forward failed
service → roxy   {"type":"response",…}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}   the client's response, exactly once
either way       {"type":"trailers","dir":"request"|"response","headers":[…]}  trailers, after the body
                 {"type":"stop","dir":"request"|"response"}               "I will read no more of this body"
                 {"type":"credit","dir":"request"|"response","bytes":n}  flow control (below)
                 {"type":"reset","message":"…"}                           abandon the stream
service → roxy   host-service calls (below)
roxy → service   {"type":"result","id":n,"value":…} or {"type":"result","id":n,"error":"…"}
```

So each stream carries four HTTP messages: the request into the service,
the request out of it, the response into it and the response out of it.
Each message is a head, then body bytes, then optional trailers, then an
end, in that order.

| rule | detail |
|---|---|
| heads | `url` is absolute. `headers` are the end-to-end headers, with no hop-by-hop or framing fields, and at most [`limits.max_headers`](/reference/limits#limits) of them. If the service sends `content-length`, its body must match it |
| header values | strings in which each character is one byte (ISO-8859-1) |
| trailers | request trailers from the service follow the rules for a client's ([trailers](/reference/http#trailers)) |
| order | the four messages are independent. The service can send its response before, during or without forwarding the request |
| errors | an end message may carry `"error"`, meaning the body stopped early and is incomplete. When the service does this to its own message it is not a fault: the flow log records `layer_aborted`, unless a fault or the client leaving came first |
| stop | `stop` tells the other side to send no more of that body. When the service stops reading the response, the upstream request is cancelled |
| end of stream | the stream ends when all four messages have ended or been stopped and all host-service calls have been answered. Either side can abandon it with `reset`, and a reset from the service fails an enforcing exchange |
| flow control | each body starts with 256 KiB of credit in each direction. The receiver grants more with `credit` as it reads. Sending more than the credit allows is a protocol error. Messages other than body bytes are not counted |
| head-only | when `subscribe` is `head` for a direction, roxy sends only the head and the service answers with only a head (or with an end alone, to send nothing). The body bypasses the service. Bytes, trailers or an end after the head fail the exchange (`unsubscribed:<direction>`) |

### Host services

A service reaches the same [host services](/reference/host-services) as a
WASM addon, by message, with the same capabilities. Each call has an `id`
chosen by the service (an unsigned 64-bit integer), and roxy answers with
a `result` carrying the same `id`: `value` is the answer (`null` for
calls that return nothing), and `error` says the call was refused.

| service → roxy | capability | roxy → service |
|---|---|---|
| `{"type":"log","id":n,"level":"info","message":"…"}` (`trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`) | `log` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"record","id":n,"kind":"…","data":<json>}` | `record` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"add_tag","id":n,"tag":"…"}` | none; enforce only | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"state_get","id":n,"key":"…"}` | `state` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":"…"}` (`null` if not set) |
| `{"type":"state_put","id":n,"key":"…","value":"…","ttl_ms":n?}` | `state`; enforce only | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"metric_get","id":n,"metric":"…"}` | `metrics` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":n}` (`null` if no count yet) |
| `{"type":"quarantine","id":n}` | `quarantine`; enforce only | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |

Calls can be sent at any time while the stream is open. They run one at a
time, in order, alongside the bodies, not in sequence with them. If an
effect must happen before something else, such as a tag before the
request is forwarded, wait for its `result` before sending that
([ordering across layers](/design/addon-model#ordering-across-layers)).
At most 64 calls can be waiting at once.

A call without its capability, a message over 64 KiB, or a tag or state
write from an observer fails the addon and resets the stream. The flow
log records the call's `id` as `call` on the events it causes. A service
makes endpoint calls itself, so there is no message for them.

### Versions

roxy offers only `roxy.layer.v7`. WASM addons use `roxy:addon@0.3.0`.

## Semantics

* **The forwarded request** is checked and judged by the rules, as a WASM
  addon's is. The response that comes back may be the upstream's, a
  refusal from the rules, or an error for a failure upstream. The service
  can pass any of these on or change them.
* **Deadlines.** `first_byte_timeout` runs from roxy's request head until
  the service answers or forwards. It pauses while the forwarded request
  is upstream, and starts again in full when the response arrives. There
  is no overall deadline on a stream, but body idle timeouts apply.
* **An early response** goes to the client at once. The upstream's
  response still arrives for the service to read, and the service's
  answer stands whatever happens upstream.
* **Failure is closed.** In enforce mode, a failed connection, a protocol
  error (bad JSON, a message out of order, a bad head, too many bytes), a
  missed deadline or a reset fails the exchange with `503` if the
  response has not started, and ends the response early if it has. The
  `layer_error` kind is `service:connect`, `service:protocol`,
  `service:timeout` or `service:closed`. A `response_end` with no
  `response` before it is `no_response`.
* **A body that fails on its way to the service is not its fault.** Its
  end carries the error, and the stream carries on.
* **A protocol error affects one stream**, unless the framing itself is
  broken (a text frame that is not a JSON object with a valid `stream`, a
  short binary frame, an unknown stream). Then the whole connection fails.
* **Observe mode** streams go one way. roxy sends copies of the request
  and response. The service sends only `credit`, `stop`, host-service
  calls, `reset`, and `{"type":"close"}` when it is done, which must come
  within `first_byte_timeout` of roxy's last message. Waiting for credit
  is falling behind, so grant generous credit when an observe stream
  opens.
* **WebSockets** run through the stream. The upstream's `101` arrives as
  the response head, and the service answers with a `101` of its own.
  After that, the request body carries the client's bytes and the
  response body the upstream's, until each side closes. roxy sends no
  `request_end` before the `101`, so the service must forward the upgrade
  as it arrives rather than waiting for the request to end.

# Host services

What an addon can ask roxy to do beyond handling its own traffic. Each
service needs a capability granted in the addon's config
([capabilities](/reference/addon-configuration#capabilities)). A WASM
addon calls them through the `flow` and `endpoints` imports. A service
layer sends the matching messages
([service layers](/reference/service-layers#host-services)). Either way
they behave the same. Size limits are in
[fixed caps](/reference/addon-configuration#fixed-caps).

## Endpoints (`endpoints`)

`endpoints.call(name, head, body)` sends a request to an endpoint named in
the addon's config. roxy adds the endpoint's configured headers, applies
its timeout, and checks the address floor. The addon cannot choose a
destination of its own and never sees the endpoint's credentials. The
call does not go through the addons or the rules, so a monitor's own
model call is not judged by itself. Each call is logged as an
`endpoint_call` event.

* An exchange can have up to 8 calls in progress. A further call waits for
  one to finish.
* The request body is buffered before the call, up to 16 MiB.
* Failures come back as distinct errors: `destination-not-found`,
  `destination-denied`, `request-uri-invalid`, `timeout` or `internal`.

The endpoint's `path` setting:

| `path` | target |
|---|---|
| `fixed` (default) | the configured URL; the path the addon gives is ignored |
| `prefix` | the addon's path, normalised, is appended to the configured path. An encoded slash or backslash (`%2F`, `%5C`) is refused |

A path segment starting with `..`, however it is encoded, is refused
(`request-uri-invalid`). With `prefix`, an addon that copies untrusted
text into the path can reach any route under the configured path, with
roxy's credentials attached.

## State (`state`)

`flow.state-get` and `flow.state-put` read and write the
[state store](/reference/rate-limits#state) that rules use. A key an
addon writes is the same key a rule reads as `state["key"]`, so an addon
can leave a mark for a rule to deny on. Values are strings. Entries
expire after one hour unless the addon sets a TTL. A full store fails the
exchange. Only enforcing addons can write.

## Identity and config

`flow.current()` returns the exchange's id, its tags, and the client as
roxy sees it: address, listener and SNI. Key per-client state on these
rather than on headers the client controls. `flow.config()` returns the
addon's `config:` as JSON.

## Record (`record`)

`flow.record(kind, json)` writes a `layer_record` event to the flow log.
Secret values are removed from it. It waits if the flow log is behind,
and is never dropped.

## Metrics and log (`metrics`, `log`)

`flow.metric-get(id, [])` reads a metric's value for this exchange's own
key. `flow.log` writes to roxy's own log, tagged with the exchange and the
addon.

## Quarantine (`quarantine`)

`flow.quarantine()` [quarantines](/guides/operations#quarantine) roxy:
the current exchange and every one after it are refused until an operator
or the control plane lifts it. Use it only when the workload must be
stopped; to refuse one request, answer it. Only enforcing addons can call
it, and a config that grants it needs `roxy run --state-dir`.

# Flow log and capture

## Flow log

The flow log is one JSON object per line, written to stdout or to
`log.flow.path`. Every exchange produces a `request` event:

```json
{"ts":"2026-10-03T10:12:00.123Z","event":"request","flow":"01J9…","conn":"01J9…",
 "listener":"proxy","client":{"ip":"10.0.0.7","peer":{"ip":"10.0.0.7","port":51234}},
 "tls":{"sni":"api.github.com","alpn":"h2","version":"1.3"},
 "req":{"method":"POST","host":"api.github.com","port":443,"path":"/repos/x/y/issues",
        "query":null,"headers_bytes":812,"body_bytes":1032,
        "body_sha256":"9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08",
        "content_type":"application/json"},
 "res":{"status":201,"headers_bytes":1420,"body_bytes":5120,
        "body_sha256":"60303ae22b998861bce3b28f33eec1be758a213c86c93c076dbe9f558c11c752"},
 "decision":"allow","rules":["github-writes"],"tags":["billing"],
 "mutations":["set_header:authorization"],"addons":["redact"],
 "timing":{"total_ms":412,"upstream_connect_ms":38,"upstream_ttfb_ms":350},
 "terminal_rule":"github-writes","stage":"head"}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `client.ip` | the client, as the rules see it |
| `client.peer` | the TCP peer the request came from. It differs from `client.ip` behind a load balancer ([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)) |
| `req`, `res` | the request as the client sent it, and the response it got |
| `body_bytes` | body bytes forwarded in each direction |
| `body_sha256` | a SHA-256 of the body, only when a rule's `digest` action asked for it ([actions](/reference/rule-language#actions)) |
| `timing.upstream_connect_ms` | time to open the upstream connection; `null` if an existing one was reused |
| `timing.upstream_ttfb_ms` | time from forwarding the request to the response head |
| `decision` | `allow`, `deny`, or `answered` when an addon answered the request itself |
| `rules` | the rules that matched |
| `terminal_rule` | what decided: a rule id, or one of `_default`, `_fail_closed`, `_address_policy`, `_expired`, `_quarantined`, `_sign`, `_websocket` or `layer:<name>` |
| `stage` | `head`, or where a rule stopped the exchange: `request_body`, `response_head`, `response_body` or `websocket` |
| `addons` | the addons that ran, in order |
| `reason` | why the exchange was refused or failed, when it was |

Common reasons, by `terminal_rule`:

| `terminal_rule` | `reason` |
|---|---|
| `_fail_closed` | `metric_unavailable`, `metric_table_full`, `address_list_unavailable`, `secret_missing`, `secret_invalid`, `body_too_large_to_inspect`, `body_decode_failed`, `unsupported_content_encoding`, `buffer_budget_exhausted`, `missing_value`, `state_unavailable`, `sign_conflict`, `effect_invalid` |
| `_address_policy` | `address_policy` |
| `_expired` | `policy_expired` ([lease](/guides/operations#lease)) |
| `_quarantined` | `quarantined` ([quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine)) |
| `_sign` | `sign_body_too_large`, `sign_header_invalid` ([signing AWS requests](/reference/secrets#signing-aws-requests)) |
| `_websocket` | `ws_bad_handshake` ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets)) |
| `layer:<name>` | `layer_error` |
| none, the upstream failed | the `upstream_error` reason ([upstream](/reference/upstream#errors)) |
| none, the exchange did not finish | `client_gone` (the client left), `client_stalled` (it stopped reading), `upstream_body_timeout` ([timeouts](/reference/limits#timeouts)), `aborted` (roxy stopped) |
| none, an addon gave up part of the exchange | `layer_aborted`: it ended the request it was passing on or the response it was giving early, or stopped reading the response from upstream |

### Events

| event | when |
|---|---|
| `request` | every exchange |
| `response_error` | the response could not be delivered after the request was allowed, for example because the client left or the upstream stalled |
| `parse_error` | the client sent a malformed request; `reason` says how |
| `upstream_error` | the upstream could not be reached ([upstream](/reference/upstream#errors)) |
| `upstream_denied` | the address floor refused an upstream address ([address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)) |
| `policy_input_unavailable`, `metric_table_full` | an exchange was denied because a policy input was unavailable |
| `policy_expired` | the policy's `valid_until` passed ([lease](/guides/operations#lease)) |
| `quarantined` | roxy was quarantined, or started quarantined (`restored: true`), with the incident `id`, `since` and `cause` ([quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine)) |
| `quarantine_released` | the control plane lifted the quarantine ([node mode](/guides/node-mode#the-lease)) |
| `upgrade_stripped` | a WebSocket upgrade was not allowed, so the request went upstream as plain HTTP |
| `ws_open`, `ws_close` | a WebSocket opened or closed, with byte counts |
| `ws_message` | a WebSocket message a rule denied, or one sampled by `log.flow.ws_message_every` ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets#message-rules)) |
| `log` | a rule's `log` action |
| `layer_error` | an addon failed; `kind` says how ([failure](/reference/addon-configuration#failure)) |
| `layer_record` | an addon's `flow.record` ([host services](/reference/host-services)) |
| `endpoint_call` | an addon called an endpoint |
| `observer_lagged` | an observing addon fell too far behind and stopped getting a copy |
| `connect` | a CONNECT, when `log.flow.connection_events` is on |
| `connection_refused` | a connection cap was reached ([limits](/reference/limits#connections)) |
| `config_loaded`, `config_reloaded`, `config_reload_failed` | startup and [reload](/guides/operations#reload) |

### Redaction

Secret values that roxy injects are removed from everything it logs. The
values of `authorization`, `proxy-authorization`, `cookie`, `set-cookie`
and `x-api-key` are never logged, and `log.redact_headers` adds more.
Query values are redacted.

### Writing

The flow log never drops a record while roxy runs
([audit backpressure](/design/threat-model#audit-backpressure)).

* One thread writes each log file, in batches, so a record is written
  within a few milliseconds.
* When more than `log.flow.high_water` (8 MiB) is waiting to be written,
  or the disk fails, roxy holds traffic until the log catches up.
* With `max_file_bytes`, the file is rotated to
  `<path>.<UTC timestamp>-<seq>`, optionally gzipped, and files beyond
  `max_files` are deleted. `SIGHUP` reopens the file, for external
  rotation.
* On shutdown roxy writes everything queued, retrying a failing
  destination for up to 10 seconds. Records still unwritten after that are
  lost.
* roxy does not `fsync`, so a power loss can lose recent records.

```yaml
log:
  redact_headers: []
  flow:
    path: /var/log/roxy/flow.jsonl  # absent = stdout
    connection_events: false
    ws_message_every: 0             # also log every Nth WebSocket message; 0 = denied only
    high_water: 8mb                 # at least 64kb
    max_file_bytes: 100mb           # absent = never rotate
    max_files: 10                   # absent = keep all
    compress: true
```

Rotation needs `path`, since stdout cannot be rotated.

## Capture

Capture records whole requests and responses to
`<capture_dir>/capture.jsonl`. It sits between the rules and the address
floor. It records the request once the rules allow it, with their
changes, and the response as it arrives from the upstream, before any
addon changes it. If the address floor or the connection then fails, the
capture holds the request head and an `end` with `aborted: true`, and no
body. It records the exchanges a rule selects
